items.title: The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth
items.content_html:
Steve Martin’s favorite comic moment of his entire career is the “hamburger” scene from The Pink Panther (2006), he once told People magazine. Martin plays Inspector Clouseau, who has an aggressively exaggerated French accent. In the scene, he is trying to learn how to say, “I would like to buy a hamburger,” with a dialect coach. “Dam-buergaaaaa,” he purrs at his coach, along with increasingly ridiculous permutations of all of the other words in the sentence.

The scene is funny because it’s true for so many of us: Learning a new language as an adult can be hard. The unfamiliar sounds may get tangled up in the mouth like marbles, and the results can sound like gibberish. But for other people, new foreign words seem to roll off the tongue and adopting different accents comes easily. Their secret may lie in how they listen, according to a new study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology. People who are better at detecting small differences in the frequency of raw sound are better at picking up new foreign speech sounds, and thus might be quicker to learn new languages, the study found.

“Read more: Speaking More Languages May Help Slow Brain Aging”

items.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
items.content_html: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.

items.title: Why your software development lifecycle is slow
items.content_html:
Traditional software development lifecycles (SDLC) were designed around how fast people could type and coordinate. Sprints, manual quality gates, and review handoffs made sense when writing code was the slowest part of the job. With AI, developers can write, refactor, and document code faster than they could two years ago. What has not moved nearly as much is how fast the same organizations actually ship.

Gartner research on AI in software engineering explains part of why. More than half of developers report that AI has improved their team’s output by 10% or less, and some see no improvement at all. The teams increasing output are applying AI across the whole SDLC, not only to the moment of writing code. When you give engineers a faster way to write code without changing anything else in the process, the result is that more code is waiting for manual reviews, which slows the path to production.

This scenario is what pushed us to rebuild our own SDLC around AI rather than layer AI on top of it. Here is what that rebuild looks like, and where most teams lose the gains before they reach the business.

KEEP IT LEAN FOR SMALL PROJECTS

For smaller projects, an AI SDLC can be simple. Before using an AI tool, write clear requirements for each feature: what it should do, what it must not do, and how the team will know it works. AI can help draft and sharpen these requirements. Store them, along with the team’s coding standards, in the same system that tracks every change to the code. That way the AI reads them as rules on every task, and they stay current after kickoff.

Then, give AI agents a narrow, well-defined scope to write and test code. A tight scope reduces the plausible-looking mistakes a model makes when it has too much room to guess. Assign a second agent or engineer to check each change against the same rules before a person signs off. The review works best when the reviewer has not watched the code being written, which keeps bias out.

WHAT CHANGES AT AN ENTERPRISE SCALE

Enterprise environments need a more robust version of the same AI SDLC because more people and more regulation are involved. On those engagements, we break business intent into three steps:

  • A high-level goal turns into a feature spec
  • A feature spec turns into individual execution tasks
  • Every piece of code and every test case ties back to the requirement that justified it

That traceability lets a team explain why a particular piece of logic exists and it gives a compliance team what it needs when an audit shows up months later. The same discipline applies to the systems the team already uses. When the AI workflow connects to ticketing tools, code repositories, and approval chains, nobody has to rebuild task lists and release packages by hand every time something ships.

The person who approves a change should never be the person who generated it. That rule already applies to human engineers on any team I have run, and AI is not an exception.

WHERE PROJECTS USUALLY FAIL

Working with AI tools introduces a new risk they can produce code and documentation in minutes forcing engineers to rush code reviews rather than slowing down at the start of the process, where the real risk sits.

The requirement and specification documents created at the beginning are the most critical part of the entire lifecycle because everything downstream inherits their mistakes. A vague or ambiguous requirement no longer produces just a vague result. It produces a fast, confident, wrong one, and by the time anyone notices, the AI has already built several more things on top of it.

Closing that gap takes discipline. Engineers and product owners must treat time spent reviewing and refining a specification as work that saves time later. Spending two extra days getting a complex requirement document right is a good trade when the old alternative was weeks of meetings to reach the same alignment. Teams at Dreamix that have adopted this structured, disciplined review process ship roughly twice as fast, without giving up code quality.

REBUILD THE PROCESS

Updating a handful of tools inside an unchanged process does not produce the gains anyone is expecting. An AI SDLC means rebuilding the process itself around where the real bottleneck exists now, which is rarely the code anymore. Get the requirements and the review discipline right, and the speed AI offers will reach the business. Skip that part, and the speed just becomes a faster way to accumulate debt.

Denis Danov is the CTO of Dreamix Ltd.

items.title: iOS 27.2 Beta 4 Removes New Health App
items.content_html:
The iOS 27.2 beta Apple released today removes the updated Health app that Apple was testing in earlier betas.


The removal of the Health app is not a surprise because Apple previously said the redesign wouldn't be introduced until late 2026.

After upgrading to the fourth beta, the Health app has a popup that says the new app features will come in a future update. Data collected during the beta remains available in the Settings app.


Apple is planning to release iOS 27.2 later in October, and the removal of the Health app suggests a launch is getting closer. The HomePod mini 2 that launches on October 30 uses HomePod software 27.2, so the updates will need to come out before that date.
